Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 60, verse 1:

(p-276) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surah al-Mumtahanah

It is Medinan by the consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun).

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, extending to them affection, while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, expelling the Messenger and you [from your homes] because you believe in Allah, your Lord. If you have come out striving in My way and seeking My approval, [then do not take them as allies], confiding to them with affection, while I am most knowing of what you conceal and what you declare. And whoever does it among you has certainly strayed from the sound way.﴾

"Al-'aduww" (the enemy) is a term that applies to both the singular and the plural, and what is meant by it here is the disbelievers of Quraysh. This verse was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, and that is because: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended to set out for Makkah in the year of the Conquest, and he concealed that by [pretending to head] toward Khaybar. It spread among the people that he was going out to Khaybar. He informed a group of his companions of his intention to go to Makkah, among them Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah. Hatib then wrote to a group of the disbelievers of Makkah informing them of the intention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward them. The news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he sent 'Ali, al-Zubayr, and a third man, said to be al-Miqdad, and said to be Abu Murthad, and said: 'Set out until you reach Rawdat Khakh, for there is a woman carrying a letter from Hatib to the polytheists.' They set out until they found the woman, whose name was Sarrah, a freedwoman of a people of Quraysh. It is also said that she was rather a woman from Muzaynah and not Sarrah. They said to her: 'Bring out the letter.' She said: 'I have no letter with me.' They searched all her baggage and found nothing. Some of them said: 'She has no letter with her.' 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not lie, nor was he lied to. By Allah, you will bring out the letter or we will strip you.' She said: 'Turn away from me.' So she untied it from the locks of her hair. It is also said she took it out from her waistband. They brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to Hatib: 'Who wrote this?' He said: 'I did, O Messenger of Allah, but do not hasten against me. By Allah, I did not do this out of apostasy from my religion nor out of desire to renounce it, but I was a man attached to Quraysh without being of their own kin, and I wished that there would be a favor for me among them by which they would protect my relatives.' 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite, O Messenger of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Hatib has spoken the truth. He is among the people of Badr, and what will make you know, O 'Umar, perhaps Allah has looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you, and say nothing to Hatib except good.' So the verse was revealed for this reason." It is also narrated that Hatib wrote: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intends to attack you in the likeness of the night and the flood, and I swear by Allah that if he attacked you alone, he would give you victory over them; so how [will it be] when he is in a great and numerous host?"

"Tulqun" (you extend) is in the position of a qualifier (sifah) for "awliya'" (allies). "Alqaytu" is transitive both with a preposition and without one, so the insertion and omission of the preposition "bi" are equivalent. This is similar to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39] and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 151]. Al-Mu'alla narrated from 'Asim that he recited: "wa-qad kafarū limā" with a lam.

His saying, may He be exalted: "yukhrijūna" (expelling) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "kafarū", and the meaning is: they expel the Messenger and expel you. It is an emphatic circumstance, which is why the verb is given in the present tense, although expulsion has already been mentioned. The restriction imposed by the disbelievers upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers is a form of expulsion, since it leads to expulsion. His saying, may He be exalted: "an tu'minū" (because you believe) is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning: they expel you because you believed in your Lord. His saying, may He be exalted: "in kuntum" (if you have) is a conditional clause whose answer is placed earlier, in meaning, than what precedes it, and this is permissible because the operation of the conditional is not apparent. The implied sense is: if you have come out striving in My way and seeking My approval, then do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies. "Jihadan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and likewise "ibtigha'" (seeking), and it is permissible for these to be objects of purpose. "Al-mardah" is a verbal noun like "al-ridha." "Tusirrūna" (confiding) is a substitute (badal) for "tulqūna". It may also be in the position of the predicate of an inceptive sentence, as if He, may He be exalted, said: you confide. It may also be a verb introduced as a new beginning of speech. Casting with affection carries a meaning of its own, and confiding with it adds a meaning beyond casting. Thus the conclusion is that "tusirrūna" is a verb begun as a new statement, meaning: you do this while I am aware. His saying, may He be exalted: "a'lamu" may be the elative form (af'al), and it may be a verb, since you say "'alimtu bikadha" and the "bi" is inserted. His saying, may He be exalted: "wa-ana a'lamu" (while I am most knowing) is a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause. The people of Madinah recited "wa-anā" with the alif lengthened when continuing the recitation, and others recited "wa-ana" with the alif dropped when continuing.

The pronoun in "yaf'aluhu" refers to the taking of allies mentioned. "Sawa'" may be an object of "dalla" (strayed), on the basis that "dalla" is transitive, and it may be an adverbial of place without transitivity, since it occurs in both ways; the first is better in meaning. "Al-sawa'" means the middle, because its relation to the extremities of a thing is equal. "Al-sabil" here means the law of Allah, may He be exalted, and the path of His religion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 60, verse 2–4:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿If they overcome you, they will be your enemies and will stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil, and they wish that you would disbelieve.﴾ ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection; He will separate between you. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you and of whatever you worship other than Allah. We have disbelieved in you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone," except for the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you, but I have not power for you against Allah at all. Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned in repentance, and to You is the destination."﴾

Allah, exalted, informed that the courting of these disbelievers is not beneficial in this world, and that it is harmful in the Hereafter, (p-279) in order to make clear the corruption of their opinion of their flattery. So He, exalted, said: "If they overcome you" meaning: if they gain power over you and you fall into their grip, enmity becomes manifest, their hands are stretched out to harm and kill you, and their tongues to revile you; and this is the evil. Yet worse than all of this is that what they seek from you is only that you disbelieve, and this is their wish.

Then Allah, exalted, informed that these ties of kinship which you desired to maintain will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection. The governing element for "Day" (yawm) is His saying, exalted, "will benefit you." Some grammarians, in the book of al-Zahrawi, said: the governing element for it is "yafsilu" (He will separate), and it belongs to what comes after it, not to what comes before it.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and the majority read "yafsilu" with a dammah on the ya', a sukun on the fa', and a light sad, vowelled with a fatha. Ibn 'Amir, al-A'raj and 'Isa read "yufassalu" with a dammah on the ya', a fatha on the fa', and a shadda on the sad, vowelled with a fatha. On these two readings there is disagreement regarding the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying, exalted, "baynakum" (between you). It was said: it is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). It was also said: it is in the nominative as the substitute for the agent of the passive, but its form remained in the accusative because this is how it was commonly used. 'Asim and al-A'mash read "yafsilu" with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the fa', and a light kasra on the sad. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Wthab read "yufassilu" with a dammah on the ya', a fatha on the fa', and a shadda on the sad with a kasra, attributing the verb in these two readings to Allah, exalted. Al-Nakha'i and Talha ibn Musarrif read "nufassilu" with the nun of majesty in the nominative, a fatha on the fa', and a shadda on the sad. In His saying, exalted, ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ there is a warning and an admonition.

The majority of the seven readers read "uswatun" (example) with a kasra on the hamza, while 'Asim alone read it with a dammah on it; the two are dialectal variants, and the meaning is: a model, a leader, and an example. "Ibrahim" (ﷺ) is the Friend of the Most Merciful, the Mighty and Majestic. People differed regarding "those with him." Some of the exegetes said: it refers to those among the people who believed in him. Al-Tabari and others said: it refers to the prophets who were in his age, peace be upon him, and close to his age. This view is more preponderant, because it is not related that Abraham, peace be upon him, had believing followers in his confrontation with Nimrod. In al-Bukhari it is related that when he, peace and blessings be upon him, migrated with Sarah to Syria, fleeing from the land of Nimrod, he said to her: "There is no one on earth who worships Allah other than me and you." This example is beneficial in disavowing polytheism, and it is consistent in every creed. In our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, there is an excellent example absolutely, because it covers the creeds and all the rulings of the Sharia.

The majority of people read "bura'a'" in the pattern fu'ala'un, the first hamza being the radical of the verb. 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "bira'un" in the pattern fi'alun, with a kasra on the ba', like karim and kiram. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read "bura'u" in the pattern fu'alun with a dammah on the fa', like tu'am. It has also been transmitted from 'Isa as a reading; Abu Hatim said: they claim it is 'Isa al-Hamdani. It is also permissible: "bara'un" as a verbal noun with a fatha on the ba', which is applied as a description to both the plural and the singular.

His saying, exalted, "kafarna bikum" means: we denied your statements and did not believe in any of them. A parallel to this is his saying, peace be upon him, relating from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "So he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the star." The feminine marker was not attached to "bada" because the feminine gender of "al-'adawa" and "al-baghda'" is not true (feminine).

Then Allah, exalted, excepted Abraham's peace be upon him seeking forgiveness for his father, and He mentioned that it was from a promise he had made; we have explained this in its proper place. This exception is not from the first part. According to Mujahid, Qatada, 'Ata' al-Khurasani and others, the meaning is that the example for you lies in this respect and not in that other one, because it was for a reason that does not apply to your situation. It may also be that it is an exception from the disavowal and the severance that was mentioned, i.e., no bond remained except this.

His saying, exalted, ﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied...﴾ up to the end of the verse is a report of the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, and those with him, that it was indeed thus.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 60, verses 5–7:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the disbelievers, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿There has already been for you an excellent pattern in them for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever turns away—indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring about affection between you and those among them with whom you have [now] enmity. And Allah is Competent, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

(p-281) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us...﴾ the verse... is a narration from Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and those with him. The meaning is: do not let them prevail over us, so that we become a trial for them and a cause of misguidance, because they would cling to their disbelief and say: "We only overcame them because we are upon the truth and they are upon falsehood." This is the meaning adopted by Qatada and Abu Majlaz. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: do not give them power over us, lest they tempt us away from our religion. It is as if he said: "Do not make us the tempted," and he expressed this with the verbal noun (masdar).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is the most preponderant of the opinions, because they were only supplicating for themselves. According to the approach of Qatada, they would be supplicating for the disbelievers. As for their aim being that the dominance of the disbelievers, which is caused by the trial of the disbelievers, be averted from them, this carries an eloquent allusion in meaning. Similar is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the Jews: "Wretched is the dead one, Sa'd," because they would say: "If Muhammad were a prophet, his companion would not have died."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There has already been for you...﴾ the verse... is an address to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying, Glorified is He: "li-man" (for whoever) is a substitute (badal) for His saying "lakum" (for you), and He repeated the preposition so that the substitution would be clear. This is the custom of such substitutions, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for the poor emigrants﴾ [al-Hashr: 8], and it is abundant in the Qur'an. The preposition most often required is "li" (the lam). Then Exalted is He informed that He is independent of worship, and that He is Praiseworthy in His essence and His actions; the disbelief of a disbeliever or the hypocrisy of a hypocrite does not diminish that.

It is narrated that when these verses were revealed, and the believers resolved to comply with their command, to sever ties with the disbelievers and to show their enmity towards them, grief overcame them over their relatives if they did not believe and were not guided, to the point that affection and kinship would exist between them. So the verse "Perhaps Allah..." came as a comfort in that regard, and as a promise that it would occur, which took place with their Islam at the conquest, and all became brothers. As for whoever mentioned that this affection was the marriage of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Umm Habiba bint Abi Sufyan, and that it was after the conquest, he erred; for the Prophet (ﷺ) married her at the time of the emigration to Abyssinia, and these verses were revealed in the eighth year after the Hijra. That is not authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), unless he presents it as an example, even though it precedes this verse, because it continued after the conquest like the other affections that arose. And "perhaps" (asa) from Allah is certain to occur, if Allah wills.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 60, verses 8–10:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being kind to them and dealing justly with them. Indeed, Allah loves the just.﴾ ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, expel you from your homes, and support others in your expulsion, that you make allies of them. And whoever makes allies of them, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, then test them. Allah is most knowing of their faith. And if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them.﴾

People differed about those whom He did not forbid you from being kind to. Mujahid said: They are the believers of Makkah who embraced Islam but did not emigrate, and for that they were in a low rank because they abandoned the opportunities of emigration. Others said: He meant the believers who abstained from emigration, who were from Makkah and from other places. Al-Hasan and Abu Salih said: He meant Khuza'a, Banu al-Harith, and tribes of the Arabs who were disbelievers, except that they supported the Prophet (ﷺ), loved him and his victory. Among them were Kinana, Banu al-Harith ibn 'Abd Manat, and Muzayna. Some people said: He meant from the disbelievers of Quraysh those who did not fight, were not expelled, and did not show evil. According to these two opinions, the verse is abrogated (mansukha) by fighting. 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He meant the women and children among the disbelievers. He also said: The verse was revealed concerning the mother of Asma', when she asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to show kindness and maintain ties with her, and he permitted her. It is reported that she was her maternal aunt, but in his narration he called her "mother." Abu Ja'far ibn al-Nahhas and al-Tha'labi said: He meant the oppressed believers who were unable to emigrate. This is a weak opinion. Murra al-Hamdani and 'Atiyya al-'Awfi said: It was revealed concerning a group of Banu Hashim, among them al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. Qatada said: It was abrogated by ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ (Q 9:5).

The words of the Exalted: "an tabarruhum" (أنْ تَبَرُّوهم) are a substitute (badal). This is the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). "Al-iqsat" (الإقْساط) means justice. "Zaharu" (ظاهَرُوا) means: they assisted. "Those who fought you over religion and expelled you" refers to the leading figures (maradah) of Quraysh.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you...﴾ The verse... was revealed right after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya. The treaty included that the believers would return to the disbelievers everyone who came to them as a Muslim, man or woman. Allah, the Exalted, then annulled this regarding women through this verse. He ruled that a believing emigrant woman is not to be returned to disbelief, but remains to undergo her waiting period (istibra') and may marry. Her disbelieving husband is to be given the dowry he had spent. He also ordered the believers to seek the dowry from those believing men whose wives had fled to them. Allah, the Exalted, ruled this way in this case. He called them "believing women" before that was certain, because that was the apparent state of their affairs. "Muhajirat" (مُهاجِراتٍ) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). "Imtahinuhunna" (امْتَحِنُوهُنَّ) means: test them and inquire into the reality of what they have.

People differed about how this testing was done. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, and 'Ikrima said: It was by the woman swearing that she did not emigrate out of hatred for her husband, nor because of an offense she had committed, nor for any worldly gain other than love of Allah, the Exalted, His Messenger (ﷺ), and the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: The testing is that she is asked to bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. When she does that, she has not come out of desire (for worldly things). A group said, including 'A'isha, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her: The testing is that the conditions mentioned in the verse after this are presented to her, namely abandoning theft, adultery, slander, and disobedience. When she acknowledges this, that is her test. It was said: This verse was revealed concerning Umaymah bint Bishr, wife of Hassan ibn al-Dahdah. In the book of al-Tha'labi, it is said that it was revealed concerning Subay'a bint al-Harith.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah is most knowing of their faith﴾ are an indication of doubt regarding some of them, and an urging to test them. The Exalted mentioned the reason why women are not to be returned to the disbelievers, which is the prohibition of intercourse and its unlawfulness. **The Word of Allah, the Exalted, the Majestic:**

﴿Give them what they have spent (as dowries), and there is no blame upon you in marrying them once you have given them their bridal payments. And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women. Ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]

﴿And if any of your wives escape from you to the disbelievers and then you have a turn (of retaliation), give those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they spent. And fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾

Allah commanded that the disbelievers be given the dowries of their women who emigrated as believers. He lifted the blame from marrying them after the giving of their bridal payments, and He commanded the Muslims to separate from disbelieving women and not to hold on to their marriage bonds. It was said: the verses concern idol-worshipping women and those whom it is not permissible to marry from the outset (ibtida'). It was also said: they are general, and the wives of the People of the Book were excluded from them by abrogation (naskh).

The word "al-'ismam" (ʿiṣam) is the plural of "'ismah" (ʿiṣmah), which means the causes of companionship and continuance within marriage. Likewise, ʿiṣmah in everything is the means one holds fast to and relies upon.

The majority of the Seven Readers and the people read "tumsikū" (تُمْسِكُوا) with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the sīn, lightened, from "amsaka." Abū ʿAmr alone, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-A'raj, and al-Hasan (in one report) read "wa-lā tumsikū" from "massaka" with the sīn doubled. al-Hasan, Ibn Abī Layla, and Ibn ʿĀmir (in the transmission of ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd) read "wa-lā tamassakū" with a fatḥah on the tā' and the mīm and a fatḥah on the sīn, doubled. al-Hasan also read "wa-tamsikū" with a fatḥah on the tā', a sukūn on the mīm, and a kasrah on the sīn, lightened.

I saw in the writings of Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī that he said: "I heard the jurist Abū al-Ḥasan al-Karkhī say, in explaining the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], that it applies to men and women." I said to him: "The grammarians do not hold this except for women, because 'kawāfir' is the plural of 'kāfirah'." He said: "What prevents this? Do people not say: 'a disbelieving group' (ṭāʾifah kāfirah) and 'a disbelieving town' (qaryah kāfirah)?" I was left speechless and said: "This is a confirmation."

Allah also commanded that the disbelievers be asked to return the charitable payments (ṣadaqāt) which the believers had given to those whose wives had fled from them to the disbelievers, and He established this ruling for all. It is reported from Ibn Shihāb that the Quraysh said: "We do not accept this ruling, we do not abide by it, and we will not pay anyone a dowry." So, because of that, this other verse was revealed: "And if any of your wives escape..." until the end of the verse. Allah commanded the believers to give to the one whose wife fled and went to the disbelievers the dowry he had spent.

Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, in the book of al-Thaʿlabī: "Five women from among the women of the emigrants (muhājirīn) turned back from Islam and joined the polytheists: Umm al-Ḥakam daughter of Abū Sufyān, who had been married to ʿIyāḍ ibn Shaddād; Fāṭimah daughter of Abū Umayyah, the sister of Umm Salamah, who had been married to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him); ʿAbdah daughter of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who had been married to Hishām ibn al-ʿĀṣ; and Umm Kulthūm daughter of Jarwal, who had been married to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him). The Prophet (ﷺ) gave them the dowries of their women from the spoils of war."

People differed over what property the dowry is to be paid from. Muhammad ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī said: it is paid from the charitable payments that were being given to the disbelievers because of those who emigrated from their wives, and Allah, the Exalted, willed to give them back to them when they did not accept His ruling, as we have mentioned. This is a sound view, required by the words of Allah, the Exalted: "fa-ʿāqabtum" (so you had a turn), and we will explain this when we comment on the word, if Allah, the Exalted, wills. Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is paid from the spoils of the military expeditions (maghāzī). They said: "al-muʿāqabah" (the taking of a turn) means the raid and the booty, and they interpreted the word in this sense. al-Zahrāwī also said: it is paid from whatever source of the fay' (spoils) is possible.

"Al-muʿāqabah" in this verse does not mean repaying evil with evil. Rather, it means: you came to be in the state in which they had been with you, and that happens when some of your wives escape to them. This is exactly the meaning of "taʿqīb" (taking turns) with a camel and riding animals, when one rides and then another rides in turn. Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "wa-in fātakum aḥadun min azwājikum" (and if any one of your wives escapes you). Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 60, verse 12–13:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you, that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children, nor bring forth a slander they have invented between their hands and feet, nor disobey you in what is right, then accept their allegiance and ask Allah's forgiveness for them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not make allies of a people with whom Allah has become angry; they have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers have despaired of the companions of the graves.﴾

This was the pledge of the women on the second day of the Conquest, at Mount al-Safa. In meaning, it was the same as the pledge of the men before the obligation of fighting (qital) was imposed. He, blessed and exalted, called them "believing women" according to the outward appearance of their affair. Rejecting association (ishtirak) is the pure essence of faith. The killing of children was out of fear of poverty, and the Arabs used to do this. Al-Hasan and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read: "yuqattilna" with a damma on the yā', a fatha on the qāf and a kasra on the doubled tā'.

As for "bringing forth slander" (al-ityan bil-buhtan), most of the exegetes said: its meaning is that she attributes to her husband a child that is not his. The wording is more general than this specification, for slandering any person by speech is a grave matter, and falsehood concerning what they have been entrusted with, such as menstruation and pregnancy, is a slander of calumny. Some are stronger than others. This is because some people said: "between their hands" refers to the tongue in speech and the mouth in kissing and the like, and "between the feet" refers to the private parts, and a child attributed to a man who is not its father, and the like. The "right" (al-ma'ruf) in which they were forbidden to disobey, Anas, Ibn 'Abbas, and Zayd ibn Aslam, may Allah be pleased with them, said: it is wailing, tearing garments, tattooing faces, joining hair, and other commands of the Sharia that it enjoined and recommended.

It is narrated that a group of women, among whom was Hind bint 'Utba, pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He recited the verse to them, and when he established them upon not associating anything with Allah, Hind said: "How can we hope that you accept from us what you have not accepted from the men?" meaning that this obligation is clear. When he reached the matter of theft, she said: "By Allah, I take a bit from the property of Abu Sufyan, and I do not know whether that is lawful for me." Abu Sufyan, who was present, said: "That is lawful for you in the past and what remains." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her: "Eat, you and your child, in a reasonable manner." This meaning is repeated in another hadith, her saying: "Indeed Abu Sufyan is a stingy man." When he reached adultery, she said: "O Messenger of Allah, does a free woman commit adultery?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her: "No, a free woman does not commit adultery." That is because adultery among the Quraysh was mostly committed by slave women, as is generally known, and by women like Hind; otherwise, prostitutes were free women. When he reached the killing of children, she said: "We raised them as small children, and you killed them when they were grown at Badr," so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed. When he reached disobedience in what is right, she said: "We did not sit in this assembly while we had in ourselves the intention to disobey you."

It is also narrated that a group of women pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we pledge allegiance to you upon such and such," the verse. When they finished, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "In what you are able and capable of." They said: "Allah and His Messenger are more merciful to us than we are to ourselves."

His saying, may He be exalted: "then accept their allegiance" means: enter with them into the bargain of faith, by which they give that from themselves and are given Paradise in return for it. The forms of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) pledging with women differed, after consensus that his noble hand did not touch the hand of a non-related woman. It is narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and others, that she said: "He pledged allegiance verbally, by word, and said: 'My saying to a hundred women is like my saying to one woman.'" And Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan said: "I was among the women pledging allegiance, and I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, extend your hand that we may pledge to you.' He (ﷺ) said to me: 'I do not shake hands with women, but I take from them what Allah has taken from them.'" Al-Naqqash mentioned a hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) extended his noble hand from outside a house, and women from the Ansar extended their hands from inside it, and they pledged. What I have presented is more established. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he (ﷺ) wrapped a thick cloth around his hand, and women came and touched his hand in that manner. It is narrated from al-Kalbi that when 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, came, the women touched his hand while he was coming out of a house, and they were inside it in a place where he could not see them. Al-Naqqash and others mentioned that the women pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ) at al-Safa in Makkah while 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was shaking hands with them. It is narrated from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, and it was raised by al-Naqqash to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and from 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi that he (ﷺ) dipped his hand into a vessel containing water, then passed it to the women, who dipped their hands into it.

Then He, blessed and exalted, commanded him to ask forgiveness for them, and gave them hope of His forgiveness and mercy by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a people with whom Allah has become angry﴾. Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: they are the Jews, because the anger of Allah, may He be exalted, has become their known attribute. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: in this verse they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, because every disbeliever upon whom is the anger of Allah, may He be exalted; this does not preclude the establishment of Allah's anger upon the Jews.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Especially among the rebellious ones, like the disbelievers of Quraysh, since their deeds are provoking anger, not merely misguidance, but there are deliberate schemings in them. In the comparison in His saying, may He be exalted: "just as," the need for this difference becomes clear, for despair of the Hereafter is either through denying it, and this is the despair of the disbelievers of Makkah, or through despairing of share and bounty in it while affirming it, and this is the despair of the Jews. Whoever says the people referred to are the disbelievers of Makkah says the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿just as the disbelievers have despaired﴾ is: just as the disbeliever despairs regarding the companions of graves, because when a close relative dies he says: "This is the last of my dealings with him; he will never be resurrected." So the meaning of the verse is that the belief of the people of Makkah about the Hereafter is like the belief of the disbeliever about resurrection and meeting his dead. This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿just as the disbelievers have despaired﴾. Whoever says the people referred to are the Jews says the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿just as the disbelievers have despaired﴾ is: just as the disbeliever despairs of mercy when he dies and is a companion of a grave, because it is narrated that when the disbeliever is in his grave, his place in Paradise is shown to him as it would be had he been a believer, and then his place in the Fire to which he is going is shown to him. So he is despairing of Allah's mercy while knowing it and being certain of it. This is the interpretation of Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Zayd regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿just as the disbelievers have despaired﴾. So the meaning of the verse is the despair of the Jews from Allah's mercy in the Hereafter while knowing it, like the despair of that disbeliever in his grave. This is because their hearts have been sealed, envy has driven them to abandon faith, and their assumptions have prevailed that they will be punished. This was the attribute of many of the contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The "min" in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from the companions of the graves﴾ is, according to the first view, for the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah), and according to the second view it is for specifying the kind (bayan al-jins) or for partitive (al-tab'id); both are possible here, and specifying the kind is more apparent.

The tafsir of Surat [al-Mumtahana] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
